lead: An image is an array of numbers. A grey image is a matrix f(x,y); x is the column, y is the row, and f is the pixel value. Arithmetic operations change the numbers, logical operations change the bits of those numbers, and geometric operations move the numbers to new coordinates. These three families are the basic verbs of image processing. They are used to average noisy phone-camera frames, subtract a background in CCTV, mask a region with bit operations, and rotate or scale a scanned answer sheet before reading it.
prereq: You need: the pixel grid and 8-bit range from 1.6, and neighbour coordinates from 1.7.

blocks.text: A digital grey image is a matrix f(x,y). x is the column index, y is the row index, and f(x,y) is the pixel value. For b bits per pixel the value lies in 0 to 2^b−1. For b=8 the range is 0 to 255, where 0 is black and 255 is white. An operation reads one or more images and writes a new image g.

Arithmetic operations work pixel by pixel. Add: g=f1+f2. Subtract: g=f1−f2. Multiply: g=f1·f2 or g=c·f. Divide: g=f1/f2. All images must have the same size, or one operand is a scalar. Guard division by zero.

The result may leave the stored range. Saturation (clipping) clamps to the nearest limit. For 8 bits, 200+100=300 becomes 255. Modulo wraparound keeps the low 8 bits, so 300 becomes 44. Use saturate for display; use modulo only when the problem states it. This is the first trap.

blocks.where: M is the number of frames; f_i is frame i; g is the averaged image. If the noise is independent with variance σ², the average has variance σ²/M and the signal-to-noise ratio improves by √M.

blocks.text: Averaging M frames of a still scene reduces random noise; the variance falls to σ²/M. Phone night mode does this. Difference |f1−f2| finds changes between two frames or a frame and a background. CCTV motion detection and PCB inspection use it.

Logical operations treat each pixel as a b-bit binary word. Bit plane k is the set of k-th bits over the whole image. AND outputs 1 only when both bits are 1. OR outputs 1 when at least one bit is 1. NOT flips every bit. XOR outputs 1 when the bits differ.

A region mask for an 8-bit grey image uses 0 and 255. 255 has all eight bits 1, so g=f AND m keeps the full pixel where m=255 and gives 0 where m=0. If a mask is stored as 0 and 1, do not AND it with a grey image: 200 AND 1 is 0, not 200. Multiply the image by the 0/1 mask, or scale the mask to 0/255, before AND. OR sets chosen bits. XOR toggles bits, so it can compare two bit planes or hide a watermark. NOT on an 8-bit image gives g=255−f.

Logical operations are not arithmetic. In the worked example 200 AND 100 is 64, not 300. Use masks to select a region before measurement, to combine bit planes, or to invert a binary image. In code, Python's &, | and ^ on non-negative 8-bit values stay in 0–255. ~ is not a fixed-width 8-bit NOT: ~200 is −201. For an 8-bit NOT write (~f) & 0xFF, which gives 55 for 200. Masks also ignore padded borders before an operation.

Geometric operations move pixel values to new coordinates. Forward mapping sends each input (x,y) to output (x′,y′). Forward mapping can leave holes whenever mapped points skip output pixels, for example scaling up or rotation. Inverse mapping visits every output pixel, computes its source coordinate, and samples the input there. Use inverse mapping for rotation and scaling.

Translation: x′=x+tx, y′=y+ty. Scaling: x′=sx·x, y′=sy·y. Rotation by θ about (cx,cy), with y pointing down and θ positive clockwise: x′=cx+(x−cx)cosθ−(y−cy)sinθ; y′=cy+(x−cx)sinθ+(y−cy)cosθ. An affine transform has six parameters and preserves parallel lines. A projective transform (homography) has eight parameters and maps lines to lines; parallel lines may meet. Document rectification uses a homography.

After inverse mapping the source coordinate is usually not an integer. Nearest-neighbour interpolation takes the closest pixel; it is fast and blocky. Bilinear interpolation takes a weighted average of four neighbours: f(x,y)≈(1−a)(1−b)f00+a(1−b)f10+(1−a)b f01+ab f11. Here f00=f(⌊x⌋,⌊y⌋), f10=f(⌈x⌉,⌊y⌋), f01=f(⌊x⌋,⌈y⌉), f11=f(⌈x⌉,⌈y⌉), a=x−⌊x⌋ and b=y−⌊y⌋. The four points are the surrounding pixels. Unit 2 covers resampling filters.

figure.caption: The tree groups the three operation families. The text gives all four examples in each family; the tree shows two per family to keep the picture readable.

spec.aria: A tree groups image operations into arithmetic, logical and geometric families, with two representative operations under each family.

examples.question: Let A = [[200, 50], [10, 240]] and B = [[100, 20], [250, 30]]. Compute (a) A+B with 8-bit saturation, (b) A AND B bitwise, and (c) A rotated 90° clockwise.

traps: Saturation vs wraparound: 200+100 is 255, not 44, unless modulo is stated.
AND is bitwise: 200 AND 100=64, not 300. Do not add.
Forward mapping leaves holes; use inverse mapping and interpolation.
Image y axis points down; check rotation sign with a corner. A clockwise 90° rotation of [[a,b],[c,d]] is [[c,a],[d,b]].
Division by zero and re-scaling: after multiply/divide, clamp or rescale; state which.

quiz.q: For an 8-bit image, state the allowed pixel range and the value of NOT for f=200.
Why does averaging M frames reduce noise?
quiz.a: Independent zero-mean noise of variance σ² becomes variance σ²/M; the signal is unchanged, so SNR improves by √M.

quiz.q: Let A=[[250,0],[10,20]] and B=[[10,5],[20,30]]. Compute saturated A+B and A XOR B.
A forward rotation by 30° leaves black holes. Explain the fix.
quiz.a: Inverse mapping visits each output pixel, computes its source coordinate, and interpolates from input pixels. Bilinear interpolation uses four neighbours, so every output gets a value and no holes remain.

quiz.q: Give one use of XOR and one use of AND on bit planes.
quiz.a: XOR compares or toggles bits, for example to find differences between two bit planes. AND extracts only the bits allowed by a mask.

quiz.q: How many parameters has an affine transform, and what does it preserve?
quiz.a: Six parameters; it preserves parallel lines.

beyond: Not for the exam. OpenCV and NumPy vectorize these operations, so a full image add is one call. In 8-bit OpenCV, cv2.add saturates; NumPy uint8 addition wraps unless you cast. Production warps use inverse maps on GPU for scanning and AR. Search next for 'OpenCV add saturation', 'warpAffine inverse map', and 'bilinear interpolation'.
